utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, can I check whether any Defence counsel wishes to cross-examine. No indication that anyone does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will now be cross-examined by Mr. Stamp on behalf of the Prosecution. Please bear in mind during your evidence today that the solemn declaration to speak the truth, which you made at the beginning of your evidence, continues to apply to your evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you still politically active?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a citizen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you a member or still a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which party is that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a member of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you hold any senior post in that party?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How long have you been a member?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were elevated in 1997 to vice-president of that party?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your information is accurate. It was then that I was elected vice-president of the Main Board of the -- vice-chairman of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia. There were five such deputy chairmen posts, and I was in charge of international relations on behalf of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In 1997, President Milosevic made a decision that there should be a reshuffling of the party leadership; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made a -- I don't know who made the decision for this new reshuffle of the party leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You're also appointed a Minister of Foreign Affairs, Minister of Foreign Affairs in 1997. Is that the year you were appointed, or 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's 1998, are you telling me then?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed federal Minister of Foreign Affairs in January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you were appointed by the prime minister, the federal prime minister?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was appointed by the Federal Assembly at the proposal of the prime minister, Rade Kontic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did President Milosevic play a role in your appointment as federal prime minister -- as federal Minister of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible, but I don't know for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were a deputy leader of the party in June 1998, or vice-president; that's the correct expression, I think.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. As I said, I was one of the co-chairmen of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, by that time, I'm sure you will agree with me, one of the main problems and issues that was facing the nation and the party was the events in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issues in Kosovo and Metohija were long-term issues. It is quite true that tensions began to mount steeply over the years that I was the co-chairman of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia and also the federal Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if there is some confusion in translation. You've twice now been translated into English as saying that you were one of the co-chairmen of the Main Board, and earlier you said you were a vice-chairman or vice-president of the Main Board. Can you clarify that for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is probably a mistranslation. I don't think I have misspoken myself. I said that I was one of the five deputy chairmen of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia; and in my capacity as deputy chairman, I was in charge of the party's international relations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: By mid-1998, the issues, the problems of Kosovo and Metohija had become central to the discussions of the party leadership at its meetings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problems of Kosovo and Metohija were without a doubt the most burning issues in both Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It was only natural that the Socialist Party of Serbia, too, as the then party in power, frequently considered what its responsibilities were vis-a-vis a political solution for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall that one of the solutions discussed at that time in the party was that senior and dependable members of the party ought to be appointed to work on coordinating the government programmes and party programmes in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. The Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia established at one point a Working Group, comprising members of the leadership of the Socialist Party of Serbia. They were tasked with dealing with the responsibilities of the party but not the responsibilities of any state organs in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of course, the Socialist Party, being the main party in the government, many of the leading members of the Socialist Party who would coordinate party work in Kosovo, were also responsible for government programmes in Kosovo because they also held government post. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of the Working Group of the Socialist Party of Serbia, in terms of their party commitments in Kosovo and Metohija, were not necessarily at the same high-ranking state officials. However, whenever there were overlaps between their individual responsibilities, there was never a dilemma. The Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia always appointed them as party officials alone, and in relation to the party's tasks and responsibilities in Kosovo and Metohija alone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall that at a meeting of the 16th session of the Main Board of the party, on the 10th of June, 1998, Milomir Minic, Dusko Matkovic, and Zoran Andjelkovic were appointed to coordinate the political activity of the SPS in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember a decision by the Main Board to set up the Working Group to deal with the party's commitments and responsibilities in Kosovo and Metohija; although, I do not remember the exact date or the exact composition. However, based on what the learned Prosecutor has just stated, it is perfectly clear that only one of the three appointees, appointed officials of the Socialist Party of Serbia, also held a post within the state structure. The remaining members did not hold any posts, or at least I was not aware of them holding any posts. For example, Dusko Matkovic, the person mentioned by the Prosecutor, to the best of my recollection, held no date post or federal post at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Minic hold a post?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Minic, at the time, was chairman of one of the councils of the Federal Assembly. However, Mr. Dusko Matkovic was only one of the deputy presidents of the party itself, that's if my memory still serves me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did Mr. Andjelkovic hold any government post in Kosovo in that period?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June 1998, which is the period you refer to, Mr. Andjelkovic was Secretary-General of the Socialist Party of Serbia. I know that much, but I can't tell you exactly when he was appointed the chairman of the provisional Executive Board of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, at that -- do you recall that meeting at all of the party, of the Main Board of the party? There was a presentation in respect to Kosovo by Mr. Minic. Mr. Milosevic also addressed the party with respect to the government programmes in respect of Kosovo, and the decision was that there needed to be more coordination of the various activities in Kosovo. Can you recall that meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must point out that the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia devoted a lot of its meetings to the problem of Kosovo and Metohija. It would be far too great a risk for me to state that I remember any specific dates or specific agendas for any of these meetings. Nevertheless, as I said, I do remember that the Main Board decided to establish its own Working Group to perform the task of the Socialist Party of Serbia in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember the party leader and President Slobodan Milosevic's address, saying the government is responsible for coordinating the work of the state organs down there, and that they've already named their representatives who will coordinate the work of the state organs?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. However, I cannot rule out that President Milosevic indeed stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you interested as a senior member of the government and a member of the -- well, a senior member of the party as well, to follow the role and the work of the government in coordinating state organs to meet the issues that were faced by the country in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not about whether I was interested or not. One of my principal duties as a member of the federal government, and in my capacity as Minister of Foreign Affairs, was to contribute to the understanding of the cause of the problems arising in Kosovo and Metohija on an international plane. Another of my duties was to explain the policies of the federal government in the Republic of Serbia to achieve a peaceful and political solution to the crisis in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I take it you're saying in the course of -- of both your party and your government functions, you never, in 1998, became aware of a body for coordinating government activities in Kosovo, in particular security forces that was referred to as the Joint Command. You never became aware of that in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I may --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P141 -- 1468.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that have a tab number in this bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No. No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my eyesight is rather poor. I have great difficulty following documents on the screen. Would it be possible for me to receive a hard copy?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist with that, Mr. Stamp, or do we have to make do with the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have to make do with the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very often, hard copy is made available, Mr. Jovanovic, but it appears there is not one available in relation to this, so the best we can do is magnify the document on the screen, and that will be done to ensure that you can read it adequately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's start with the page in front of you. Can you read that? This is a document. The front page reads "Meetings of Joint Command of Kosovo and Metohija."

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may just make an observation. This is a very unusual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wouldn't it be fair to first ask the witness if he's ever laid eyes on this document? The title page was shown, and it went missing from the screen without the witness telling us whether he's actually seen the document or not. I believe that would only be fair and even required, wouldn't it, for this to be shown him and for him to be told what is exactly he's being shown. There. I don't, as a matter of principle, oppose the idea of the witness being shown this, but I think he should be told what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you realised that he was about to tell us that it was of an unusual nature. We'll let the witness proceed with the answer, Mr. Fila. Please continue, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's fine, as far as I'm concerned. This is a very unusual document. It's a handwritten document which has no header; not the sort that one usually expects to find in an official document. I can only see a portion of what the Prosecutor claims is a title page. I can't even see the title page in its entirety, and particularly, I can't see the bottom of the page, or the substance, or for that matter of signatures and stamps. Therefore, what I can observe, based on this, is that a document like this, for example, in Serbia's legal system, would have no legal consequences or importance whatsoever. May it be understood that I've never set eyes on this document before, this handwritten document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to see if you could read what's on the screen, the document. It states --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I can read. I'm a literate person. If I get legible documents to read, I'm perfectly able to read them as a rule, and not just in my language; I dare say, in a number of different languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. I understand that. You see the document purports to be relating to the meeting of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija on the 22nd of July, 1998? Do you see that on the document?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm perfectly able to read what the text says. I'm a lawyer by training. To me, as a lawyer, this does not have the appearance of an official document, not in terms of its form, not in terms of its substance, not in terms of how it was technically produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Jovanovic, I'm going to ask you just to confirm your answer to what I've asked you. I understand what you're saying, but those issues as to authenticity and source of this document are issues which can be dealt with otherwise. You said you have of never laid your eyes on this document before. Now, do you see some names there on this document as being present at this meeting? Do you see that, a list of persons named?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we scroll down, please, so we can see the entire list? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was number 8, Milan Djakovic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, don't hold it against me, but I've never met this person or anyone by that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But you have met Mr. Minic, Mr. Sainovic, Mr. Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Without going into these documents, since you haven't seen them before, I'm going to represent to you that these documents purport to indicate that there were very frequent meetings of this organisation in 1998, which Mr. Sainovic would attend with senior police and military figures; and in many of these meetings, he would define the issues, some of what is happening, and give instructions. I represent that to you. Now, the question is this: Were you aware of Mr. Sainovic, in any capacity, attending meetings in 1998 with senior military or police officers present? When I say "senior," I mean of the rank you see here, like General Pavkovic and General Lukic.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as I've said, I've never set eyes on this document before. I never attended any such meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, if I could stop you just for a moment. As a lawyer, you'll appreciate that, when one is investigating allegations of crime, the inquiry is not confined simply to official documents. This document has featured once or twice in this trial, and the question of its authenticity will be dealt with separately. We've heard that you've never seen it before. We understand that. The question that you were asked is a perfectly simple question, and you were being given an opportunity to see what's available before being invited to answer it, which is a fair way of proceeding, and the simple question was whether you were aware of Mr. Sainovic, in 1998, attending meetings with senior military and police figures. Now, that doesn't depend on the document; that depends on your recollection. And if you could help us with that, it would be extremely useful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I waited for the question and the answer to be over. I didn't intervene because I do not mind the way Mr. Stamp phrase the his question, but what did this question mean, that Mr. Sainovic took part in Joint Command meetings, because this paper is right under his nose, or should this paper be removed from the screen and should the question be put as follows: Did Sainovic ever attend such meetings? Because if you look at this paper, it's only fair to assume that he attend the meeting that is in front of you. That is what I wanted to say in terms of procedure. You cannot show one piece of paper and ask a question that relates to something completely different. That is my objection, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If, however, you were listening closely, Mr. Fila, you would note that's how I put the question. I diverted the attention of the witness away from the document and ensured that he was answering the general question, and he's answered by saying no. No matter whether meetings were joint command or anything else, he was not aware of Sainovic, in 1998, attending meetings with senior military and police figures. So that's a complete blank as far as the Prosecutor is concerned. Mr. Stamp, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, that's what I've been saying, that you had to intervene because the Prosecutor is not doing it right. So lest this happen again, that was all I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, were you aware of Mr. Sainovic attending meetings on a regular basis with the leadership of the VJ and the MUP in Kosovo and Metohija in 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This -- if that happened at all, it did not come within your remit? You would not know about it, or you're saying that would not have happened at all?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the answer I gave. I am not in favour of dealing with any kind of hypothetical situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the course of your association with the party, was it not -- well, let's not say "frequent." May I rephrase the question. On occasion, did not President Milosevic make arrangement in respect of the work of the government that were not necessarily on official lines?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is only one type of government sessions; namely, those that are scheduled by the prime minister. I am not aware of any other type of government meetings that anyone else called at any other time, officially or informally.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- for example, just as an example, did President Milosevic informally, without official documentation, ask the former chief of the customs in Serbia to deliver to you 900 [sic] marks in cash?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a malicious question counting on my -- or, rather, intending to discredit me personally and my testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quite understand whether the proceedings here have to do with the problems in Kosovo and Metohija or the work of the customs office -- the federal customs office in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In spite of that, would you please answer the question, and we'll judge whether it's got any significance for the determinations we have to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Allow me, Your Honour, to say that I am 69 years old, that I lived in five states, and was the citizen of five states in the territory of Yugoslavia. I lived under five different social-political systems, and never until this point in time have I been convicted in any kind of proceedings, criminal or civil.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand what you say. Are you unwilling to answer the question, because it's a perfectly simple one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question well then. Could it please be repeated?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The question is simple: Did President Milosevic informally ask the head of the customs department, Mihajl Kertes, to hand you 900,000 marks from customs revenue in cash?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a different question than the one that's on the screen, which related to 900 marks, or it may be a translation -- no, it can't be. It's your own language, it's your own words that are being recorded, and that's what I heard. I didn't hear anything inconsistent with the transcript. And if it's such a significant allegation as the one you now make, can you put a date on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The figure of 100.000 [sic] or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let me just ask you one question. It's an important -- it is -- and I just say this. I intend to make no allegations. I'm just going to ask you open questions that I invite you to answer. You gave a statement, in regard to what I'm asking you about, to a judge, didn't you? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tell the Honourable Court the following, that investigations are secret in the country that I used to live in, Yugoslavia. And everything that witnesses say during the course of the investigation cannot be disclosed. If Mr. Stamp wants to use that transcript, I was counsel. I know what this is about. Let him show me a waiver issued by the state of Yugoslavia that he's allowed to disclose this document. I, as Defence counsel, was not allowed to use that. Please look at the heading there, and you will see that I'm Defence counsel, and that cannot be used. He can ask him something, but he cannot put this to him.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Stamp's microphone please be turned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for these proceedings, they were stopped against Milosevic because he died. So you have to have grounds for this; otherwise, I am going to show the documents that you have forbidden me to use. The Serbian press could hardly wait to read these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that we can address this properly, we shall go briefly into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, there's a fine line here that I'm not sure where it should be drawn. If a cross-examiner asks a question of a witness based on a document which he has received from somewhere, he could certainly be required to prove that he had some kind of a basis for asking the question. The question that I have is: At what point. When you're using a document in that way. Should it be a document that's notified to the Defence, as all other documents that are going to be used on cross-examination are notified to the Defence? No notice was made that this particular document would be used, yet I watched Mr. Stamp stand up there and hold it in his happened and refer to it as a document that he was using during this cross-examination. If he was going to use it during this cross-examination, then he should have made it available to us and told us he was going to use it, in my view. The second part is -- is another part of that, and give me just a second to find it. During his explanation to you of what he was doing,

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP SAID THIS
utterances.text: "There are few occasions where you have a document or evidence because is -- it is informal. One occasion, the Prosecution will later allege, is a situation in respect of the Joint Command, and this is another situation which fortuitously we laid our hands upon." I suspect that he's talking about another document regarding the Joint Command, and I don't see that noticed in the cross-examination for this witness, and I don't know if it's been finished to us. But we understood the rule as we were doing cross-examinations of their witnesses that we were to notify them of every document that we'd use and make it available to them, and we did that. If we had thought we could ambush witnesses like this, we would have been doing that. That doesn't do much for justice, but it makes for a more fun trial, I suppose. But I don't think this is proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Deal with the second point first, please, Mr. Stamp. Are you referring to yet another document later?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. When I said "fortuitously we have a document," indicating some informal arrangement, I was referring to this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I understood certainly. So that deals with the second point. On the first point?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The first point, the document we propose to cross-examine the witness: The documents that base this question were disclosed to the Defence, and we advised them that the documents could be used in cross-examination. Perhaps my friend didn't link the P number in e-court to the particular documents. Ambush is a strong word. We have no intent of ambushing the Defence. I make that clear. So the documents were given to the Defence and I don't even -- I hope not even to use the documents. Many times, the documents are put there, and the witness answers a certain way. We move on without using the document. Having regard with what Mr. Fila said, it is not my intention to use any of these documents with the, witness unless absolutely necessary. They are there for a very limited purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman that seems to answer the first point also.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What exhibit number is that interview that Mr. Stamp has been referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. I apologise, I wasn't aware of that particular exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can the witness please return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we are often guided by counsel who object when inappropriate questions are posed. We often act ourselves, without prompting, to refuse to allow a question to be posed; and with that background, we would be grateful if you would allow us to be the judges of what questions you should and should not answer. Having had a chance to reflect on this issue, we consider that it is appropriate for the Prosecutor to seek an answer to the question he posed to you, which with a date added to it or a rough time scale would, in our view, be a perfectly reasonable question to put in the context in which he seeks to put it. So please listen, again, to the question from Mr. Stamp, and please assist us to the best of your ability with an answer based on your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Just before the issue goes completely away, P2897, which is the document he's referring to, is only in Serbian. There's no English translation, which explains why I probably didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We weren't holding it against you, Mr. Ackerman, and your explanation confirms we were right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand, but there still should be an English translation of it if he's going to use it, I would think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it looks as though he's not, so let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could I just say that P2898 is in English and, indeed, is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before we lose the thread of this completely, could you please pose your question, and let's hear what Mr. Jovanovic has to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, if you can, could you just answer yes or no. Did Mr. Milutinovic -- withdrawn. Did Mr. Milosevic ask the head of the custom department to deliver to you $900.000 in cash, in the first half of 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In May 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware what Mr. Milosevic told Mr. Kertes to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Did Mr. Kertes - and this is a slightly different question, which you can answer yes or no as well - in the year 2000, hand over to you a total of approximately 1.4 million marks in cash?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this money was not handed over to you in the normal course of government business, or by "normal" means through the budget and the ministry, but it was an informal arrangement to achieve various goals?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was not an informal arrangement; rather, I received that money belonging to the state as the federal Minister of Foreign Affairs for the needs of the state. And the money was partly spent to meet the needs of the state, and the rest remained in cash in the Foreign Ministry of foreign affairs during and after the changes of October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave, I wish to stress that while I was Foreign Minister for Foreign Affairs, every cent of state money I received was invested for the needs of the state exclusively, and there was not the smallest possibility for anyone to misuse state money for their personal or private purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Now, Mr. Jovanovic, please understand me. I'm not, in the next question, suggesting at all that you or anybody misused the money. That's a question for a different forum. All I want to know is whether or not this money was handed over to you in the normal method, through the normal financial systems in place at the government, or was it an informal arrangement for that money to be handed from the customs, duties, in cash?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, formally, there was no normal banking system in Yugoslavia. The money was handed over officially by one official of the federal state to another official of the federal state with the appropriate documents accompanying the money, which made it possible to trace the course of the money from the moment it entered the Foreign Ministry of -- Foreign Ministry until it was invested for certain purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What position did Mr. Kertes hold then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Kertes at that time was the director of the Federal Customs Administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see your explanation here, but -- and, again, I remind you. All I'm asking about is whether or not the hand-over of the money was according to the normal system of budgetary administration in the government. I'm not asking you about any possible use of it. Did you explain to the judge who interviewed you why the cash --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, that's a matter that we understood you were not necessarily embarking upon, and we've heard certain things said about it and may wish to hear more. Can't you ask this in an open way at the moment? Must you take the line that you're about to take, because there may then be reasons for going into private session or taking a different line.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not to tell you, you can't do it; it's to tell you to be cautious in how you do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They well. I'll ask just one other question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your career in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, have you ever received cash to the tune of a million marks or more for government business, apart from this occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received that money only when I was Foreign Minister -- the Federal Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that was the only one time that you received cash money for government affairs -- sorry, you received cash in that quantity, in that amount for government affairs? Only one it happened in your entire career?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm certainly not clear about this, because I don't think it was very clearly put to you. Is that the only occasion on which you received a large amount of cash for official ministry business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The amount mentioned here was handed over to me on three occasions. In any case, I received certain amounts of money from Mr. Kertes on three occasions. On each of those occasions, the hand-over was carried out with the appropriate accompanying documents which are in the state archives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Roughly, what were the dates of these occasions, these three occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot remember the dates. If the Prosecutor has the documents, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The year then? Can you assist us with the year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was in the year 2000. I received the first amount for repairs to the ministry building, the roof of which had been destroyed in the NATO aggression. On the second occasion, I received funds to prepare -- to repair a state building intended for foreign diplomatic representative offices. And on the third occasion, it had to do with the sending of a large number of diplomats to assist in Rambouillet and Paris during the so-called negotiations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, these negotiations were in 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went on until January 2000 and were completed only later, I think, in March. I think the negotiations finished on the 19th of March, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour. No, it was 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, was that the last of the three payments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from those three occasions, there were no other payments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one Mr. Stamp first asked you about was in May 2000, which is significantly later than the use of money for attendance at Rambouillet and Paris.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot recall the date. It's quite possible this happened in May. I would be assisted by documents if the Prosecutor could show them to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you just clarify the amount on each of these three occasions for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know, on one occasion, it was about 500.000 marks. On the second occasion, it was probably these 900.000 mentioned here. And on the third occasion, I cannot remember the amount. In any case, I wish to point out that every detail, including the amount and date, is recorded in documentation, official documentation, in the Foreign Ministry, the Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and these documents can be used if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know whether the work of any other ministry was being funded in this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There is one other question I have on this issue. You remember, though, that all of this money was handed over to you in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the dates. Could I please be shown the documents on the basis of which such documents are being asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was not saying about the date. I was saying about the year, the year 2000. Do you remember it was all in the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been given quite contrary evidence to that, that one of these was prior to the 19th of March 1999. You may have stumbled upon a nugget, or it may be something in relation to material that you already have. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, may I say that I would not like to speculate. In my opinion, it would be best to look at the official documentation of the Foreign Ministry of foreign affairs. I believe that the esteemed Prosecutor has these at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, your counsel will -- Mr. Sainovic's counsel will have an opportunity to re-examine you at the end of the Prosecutor's cross-examination. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You testified -- I am moving on. Do you testify that it was the policy of the government of the FRY to solve the issues in Kosovo, in 1998, through dialogue and peaceful means? And you discussed with us yesterday a number of documents which someone from the government of the FRY used that -- used that expression, that it was intention to solve the problems through peaceful political means. We have a number of witnesses here who said that that is what was regularly, naturally being said by the FRY government officials; for example, Wolfgang Petritsch. But he testified that part of the problem was that what was being said was contradicted by what was happening on the ground. Did any of your three outposts in Kosovo and Metohija, in 1998, report upwards to you, the minister, about alleged crimes that were committed by the Serbian MUP or the VJ against Kosovo Albanian citizens in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the Prosecutor is in a better position because he can hear witnesses I have not had an opportunity to hear, but I knew them as diplomats of their countries in Belgrade. My points in Kosovo and Metohija, my outposts, never reported that there was ever any kind of violence or illegal work being done by the security services or the organs of Serbia or the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, in fairness to you, perhaps I should remind you that that question was about allegations of crime. So are you saying that none of your outposts even reported allegations against Serb forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My outposts faithfully transmitted the contents of conversations conducted by them or other diplomats with foreign diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija, and they conveyed the comments or complaints against actions of the state organs in particular situations as these were seen and assessed by foreign representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did that include allegations of criminal activity by Serb forces or person he will?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I think these were incidents and accusations, for example, concerning the massacre in Racak. Of course, the diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija reported such accusations to the head office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the question so far has related to 1998, which is earlier than Racak. Were such reports being received of accusations against Serb personnel in 1998?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such comments by foreign representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, is this a suitable time to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we have to take a break at this time. In fact, I think you were with us yesterday when we had to have a similar break. The usher will show you where to go while we have this break. In this instance, it will simply be 20 minutes. We will resume at 10 minutes to 11.00. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When we left off, you said that there were comments by foreign representatives in respect to accusations received about the activities of Serb personnel. In regard to that, Mr. Jovanovic, we have evidence for the Court that in the course of the operation, in 1998. And "1998," I'm speaking of evidence from one Mr. John Crosland, who was with the KVM in Kosovo, and his evidence is P2645 for the record. He saw hundreds of villages burnt. Crops were wantonly destroyed. Business of all sorts were looted and destroyed. Those are the types of reports or allegations that he received up the chain or through diplomatic channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were those -- did you receive information about complaints like that being made by the foreign diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The showdown with terror groups in Kosovo and Metohija certainly led to casualties, and, as is well known, not just on one of the sides. There is one thing that I wish to point out. As a minister and a citizen of the Republic of Serbia, I bow before the shadows of all victims, and I think that whoever is responsible must be made to account for all these victims. As for all the reports on burnt villages and similar events, if any such reports reached my office, they were swiftly forwarded to the relevant bodies for verification so that appropriate measures might be taken. Our role in this was to collect all those reports on positive and negative trends alike in Kosovo and submit them without undue delay to the relevant bodies. We always displayed great earnestness in performing this task. As for Colonel Crosland's evidence, I'm not familiar with his reports, nor were the reports of foreign delegates [as interpreted] ever forwarded to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the foreign military observers. May I just add this: The diplomatic representatives of my ministry in Kosovo and Metohija, as a rule, were not in contact with military officials but with civilian representatives alone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, page 32, line 5. The witness said "military attaches."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Instead of "foreign delegates"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, when you say that, as a minister and a citizen of the Republic of Serbia, you bow before the shadows of all victims and think that whoever is responsible must be made to account for all their victims, is that an expression of acknowledgement now that there were victims for whom some Serbs bear responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no doubt whatsoever that crimes were committed on all sides. It remains to be established who the responsible persons for those crimes were. There were certainly crimes committed by Serbs as well; however, this was never a policy pursued by the government of which I was a member. This was never a policy pursued by Yugoslavia or Serbia, generally speaking. These were crimes committed by individuals, individuals who acted in a random and wanton manner and were under no kind of control. As far as I know in very general terms, because this is not my sphere of activity, proceedings were instituted in many of these cases in order to establish the criminal responsibility of all those suspected to be responsible for crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the cabinet on occasions discuss this, the problem of allegations of criminal behaviour by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware if and when this sort of problem was included in the agenda of the federal government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm curious. If the allegations were taken seriously, were they not significant enough for the government to discuss them, with a view to deciding how to at least present a better face to the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is understood that, in these cases, those bodies and those institutions came into play that bore legal responsibility for doing something about any crimes that were committed. I am talking about the institutions of the judiciary, first and foremost, as well as state investigators and prosecutors. As for considering these problems at a political level, it goes without saying that, in the framework of analysing the general situation and problems in Kosovo and in terms of adopting general positions, the government had occasion to familiarise itself with this sort of problem. It also had occasion to react in an appropriate way. I'm afraid I can't be more specific, simply because I can't name the specific sessions or the specific dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sir, did the members of the government -- well, did you, for example, and President Milosevic discuss the idea of razing to the ground any area in respect to KLA activity?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is understood --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you or did you not? I'm sorry. We have to move a little bit quickly. Did you have discussions like that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I respect the need for expedience, but it is certainly not in your best interest to be denied a full answer, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Fila will no doubt ask any relevant follow-up questions, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could we put on the e-court P2 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for your last question -- as for your last question, my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- P2899, and if I could with the help of the usher hand the witness a hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First and foremost, can we have the witness leave the courtroom for a brief while so we have a chance to discuss this? One look at the document should be sufficient for you it to understand why I am requesting this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can it be shown on our screen, first of all? Mr. Jovanovic, we've been asked to invite you to leave the courtroom to discuss this, and we think that's an appropriate course to follow, so could you go with the usher. We'll be as quick as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document served on us by the OTP under Rule 68, exculpatory material. I'm not sure what it's supposed to exculpate anyone from, but this is an intercepted conversation. You can't tell, on the face of the document, who it was intercepted by or when, nor what the technology was that was used. I now remind you that the OTP originally had on their list witnesses who were supposed to tell us who they were intercepting, who they were eavesdropping on how and when, but the OTP never produced those witnesses that were promised. This document, if indeed it deserves to be called a document, cannot be used as a basis for this, because it shows none of the things that it's supposed to tell us: Who, when, how. This is a shred of paper that I don't think is worth discussing. They said they would bring witnesses to tell us about these intercepts, tell us how, when, and who, but they failed to do that. Therefore, I don't think this document should be used. Anyone could have put it together. We first set eyes on it two days ago. I'm not suggesting that Mr. Stamp put this document together. That is not at all what I'm suggesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you saying this was disclosed to you only two days ago as Rule 68 material?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right, under Rule 68 as exculpatory material, without knowing exactly what it is. It's a shred of paper as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the -- my learned friend is not making an appropriate distinction between two matters in respect to the use of documents of this nature. One is whether or not the document as it is now can be used as evidence, and perhaps not. That is one question. Another question is whether or not a witness can be asked a variety of questions about the document, which is what the Prosecution purports to do now, and this is not any witness. This witness is a lawyer, and the document can be used to ask him to refresh his memory and can be used to ask him if the contents are true. So I submit that use of the document for cross-examination is quite permissible. Whether or not the document, as it is, can be used as evidence of the truth of its contents is a different question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you asked him questions on which you need to refresh his memory?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I've asked him about whether or not they discussed razing an area, and I would also ask him about the circumstances surrounding the purported conversation or the conversation that the document purports to -- to record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the other matter raised with you is the time of disclosure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This document came to our -- has been in our records, I admit that, but it came to our attention in recent searches done by what is called the ISU, the search unit of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I know within a matter of days before or maybe the same day when it was disclosed. I mean, I could estimate when we received it from that unit or when it was located based on the system that we have. When a witness is coming, the ISU, we ask them to do searches of the millions of documents that we have, and also searches in the internet on that person. And sometimes it brings up documents we did not know before. So the results of this search had become available to us sometime within days before the witness came in, maybe sometime last week, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How long has it been in the possession of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Since the 22nd of September, 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it couldn't be said to be obvious that any intercepted communication of Slobodan Milosevic might have relevance for this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I certainly think that any intercepted conversation of Slobodan Milosevic in respect to Kosovo would be relevant to this trial, and therefore this is on its face relevant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but it makes it very strange that it has not been discovered earlier. All you need to put in is Milosevic, intercepted communications. Would you not to do an exhaustive search for that in the course of preparing for this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm quite sure that searches have been conducted for that on more than one occasion. It is possible when it comes to searching electronic photo records, not word documents or documents -- or digital documents, when the search tool has to scan the document for the word, that sometimes the words are missed and the technology improves every day, as it were, but I can't explain how the document was missed. I just know that it happens from time to time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one thing with. In order to call something a document in a legal sense - and we are lawyers, aren't we? - there must be a foundation. What I choose to call this is a shred of paper. It wasn't given to me for me to investigate it, and this is not the first case of something like this happening. Some witnesses we received on the 15th of July, then some other witnesses were found at a very late date, and then they found some additional witnesses which they forwarded to us. But I'm questioning the method used because we did not apply this method in dealing with them. Secondly, we talked about the sensitivity of intercepts. They said they would bring the people who did the actual intercepts, which they failed to do. As a consequence, I am now made to suffer and bear the brunt. I don't think that would be fair. They did promise that. They did promise that the people who made the intercepts would be coming forward on their behalf. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The document appears to have disappeared from the screen. Can it be returned? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, what indication is there that this is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: On the face of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, or because it's been certified or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The evidence unit of the OTP makes a receipt or a record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I mean, when I talk about certificate, I mean on the face of it. How can we tell at this point that this is an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The contents of the document. One is the contents of the documents. It would indicate that this is a document, a record of a transcript of an interview -- or a transcript of a tape recording of an interview. I don't know if in these circumstances, we would expect the document to be stamped or anything like that. But I would concede that, on its face, there is no direct indicia of authenticity of the document. And that is a matter, I respectfully submit, that would weigh in an issue as to the admissibility of the document later on, or the use of the contents of the document for the truth there. However, the witness can be shown the document and be asked about the circumstances in which a conversation might have occurred and whether or not, having seen the document, he recalls the conversation and what was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the moment, we're not satisfied that it was necessary for you to get to this point at this time. This is a matter that could have been explored orally with the witness before any question of refreshing his memory arose. What's the problem about dealing with it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It could be dealt with that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, we shall allow you to ask questions orally of the witness and hope that the matter can be dealt with that way, and we see no need at this stage for his being referred to the document, so let's have the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the document should be removed from e-court, please, that's from the display. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall participating, in January 1999, in efforts to secure the release of some Serb -- or some VJ personnel who were held by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, it's hard for me to remember because there were a lot of kidnappings - military, police, and civilian at that - by the terrorist KLA. Sometimes I did have a role in seeking ways and means for these persons to be set free, but most often this was done through other ministries and other institutions, because I was focused on contacts with foreign diplomats, primarily in Belgrade and in other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've been given the impression that this was a well-known incident in January 1999, where there had to be an exchange of prisoners, and it had to be undertaken in a particularly sensitive way. Do you not remember that? I think eight Serb soldiers were detained, and there were a number of KLA prisoners to be swapped over for them. Are you saying you don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. The question put here was whether I took part in setting them free, not whether I remember the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I won't bandy words with you, Mr. Jovanovic, but I think you could have answered the question in a simpler way, if you do clearly remember the incident. Do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you remember making contact with diplomats in Belgrade for the purpose of securing the release of the soldiers who were held?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember any specific case when I acted --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm talking about the case in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that case, and it is quite possible that I was involved in the process of their release, but I do not remember that this was in the form of exchanging prisoners of war, because I don't know what kind of prisoners of war could be involved when I do not know what the warring parties are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I don't think I used the expression "prisoners of war." I referred to "prisoners." If you wanted to change that to some other expression, I'll happy agree to it, if we can just get to the crux the matter and not get bogged down in technical definitions. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As the Foreign Minister of the federal republic, did you play any part in any diplomatic discussions in relation to the release of these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, that, Mr. Jovanovic, appears to be a quite different answer from one you gave a moment ago, when you said you were possibly involved. Please concentrate on these questions and ensure that, at the first time of asking, you answer with the full extent of your knowledge. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you discuss your role in making contact, diplomatic contact, with President Milosevic -- I withdraw the question. Let me rephrase the question. Did you have conversations with President Milosevic about what you were doing in contacting foreign diplomats about releasing these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that I talked to President Milosevic about that, but I did everything I could in contacts along my own lines in order to set the kidnapped soldiers free.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a diplomat in Belgrade at the time that you referred to -- or referred to as "Miles"?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the charge d'affaires of the US embassy, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you or your ministry get in touch with Miles to discuss this issue?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, because the UN diplomat had influence over the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, incidentally, what is Miles full name?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not recall. I just know it's Miles, and that he was the charge d'affaires of the US --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let the question be answered, then we'll come back to transcript problems. Sorry, about that, Mr. Stamp, but I think you've got the answer, though, that the witness doesn't know his full name. Now, Mr. Zecevic, what's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's been cleared in the meantime, Your Honour. UN, US.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall telling Mr. Milosevic about the course of these discussions that you were having with the Americans on the 9th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not remember that I talked about this with President Milosevic. I simply do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Milosevic telling you to keep Saho [sic] posted about the developments?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, twice, he said that he did not remember talking to Mr. Milosevic. How could he remember the details of something that he does not remember in the first place? This is really too much now; I think, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we disagree. We've considered this carefully in the period we had, and we consider that to try to refresh the witness's memory in this way is entirely appropriate. So please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Sainovic was referred to as "Saho"; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I am not aware of that being correct. I never called him by that nickname or did I ever hear anyone call him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was he referred to as "Sajo"?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that either. I don't know. I always called him "Sainovic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What about other people? Did you ever hear anyone else call him by a shortened form of his name or a sort of a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't hear that. I have already told Your Honour that, as far as I'm concerned, my relations with Sainovic were always official; and in these relations, I never used any nicknames or any abbreviated versions of names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you tell Mr. -- well, do you recall telling Mr. Milosevic, in respect to your dealings with the Americans, that you told Mr. Sainovic about it?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall Mr. Milosevic, if Mr. Milosevic told you, in conversation about these captured soldiers, that he told Sainovic that he, that is, Mr. Sainovic, could give them, that's the KLA, six hours?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you not recall in the course of this conversation Mr. Milosevic saying that, "We should try this," that is, give them six hours, and, "If not, we'll raze them to the ground"? Do you recall Mr. Milosevic saying that at all to you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall, or knowing President Milosevic does it seem to me that he could have said anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you recall suggesting to Mr. Milosevic that you should also speak to the Russians about what is happening?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you, as a minister, contact the diplomats on behalf of Russia to speak to them about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a moment, please, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I wonder if you could again leave the courtroom very briefly. There is something I want to ask about this, and I want to do it without your presence. There is nothing usual about that course of action. I'm sorry you have had to go in and out more than once, but this will be very brief.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you have the actual recording of the intercept?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I've got a transcript in the same organisation that was the subject of applications that were made earlier in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Have you now completed the points you're making to the witness from the material?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're not inclined to allow you to place this document before him, because there is no foundation for saying at this stage that it is authentic. On the other hand, if you had had the recording, the position would have been quite different, because you could have put to the witness the question whether it was his voice. However, if we've completed that, we can move to something else. Bring the witness back, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you for your patience, Mr. Jovanovic. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, I'm going to ask you to bear with me. There are some other matters I think we need to move through rather quickly in regard to the time. Do you remember the date that Mr. Sainovic left Rambouillet to return to Belgrade for consultations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this at the beginning of the talks there when the issue as to the signing of the principles, the ten principles, was raised?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that that happened at the moment when the negotiations -- or rather, the process in Rambouillet got into a very serious crisis. I remember very well that his trip had to do with consultations as to how this critical point in time should be overcome in order for the negotiations to continue. However, with all due respect, please understand me that, as a rule, I have difficulty with remembering dates, and, of course, all of this happened eight years ago. So it is impossible for me to remember the date or even the time frame as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But it was in relation to issue of the signing or non-signing of the ten principles, ten non-negotiable principles of the Contact Group? Was it in relation to that that he returned to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The discussions leading up to Rambouillet lasted for a period of many months in 1998. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you participate in those discussions?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some of them in Belgrade, yes. As a rule, whenever I was in the country, when I was not on foreign visits, then I did take part in these talks. However, in other places like Pristina or, generally speaking, places outside Belgrade, I did not take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were you aware that sometimes the Contact Group, for practical purposes of achieving progress in the discussions, would sometimes hand over various chapters to be discussed at different times -- or maybe I should withdraw that and quote directly from the evidence. In order to achieve advancement in the discussions, sometimes the Contact Group had the policy of handing over draft agreements, chapter by chapter, in order to hold focus and make progress, were you area of that, in the course of the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did the not know that those were the methods used, let alone that these were decisions of the Contact Group, but that is precisely what was done in Rambouillet. As for the integral text, it was published in a newspaper in Albanian in Pristina before the negotiations in Rambouillet started. Therefore, the question is why something which was basically published as a integral text, as the entire text, in Pristina was being distributed only in its parts in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. That is not responding to any question I asked you, and I'm not sure if you're asking me that. But the evidence of Mr. Petritsch is that the entire text was formerly known to the parties at Rambouillet from at least the 18th of February. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During 1998, was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a member of the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you had representatives at the OSCE headquarters in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an embassy in Vienna that was at the same time in charge of our relations with the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I give a brief explanation, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Of what?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you feel you need to explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was never expelled from the OSCE. Its membership rights were temporarily suspended for a certain period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Was it suspended in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thanks. Are you aware that KVM mission reports went to the headquarters in Vienna and from there were distributed to the Member States, including the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have already had occasion to tell Your Honours that one of the key problems in cooperation during the KVM mission consisted in the fact that the OSCE was not carrying out its obligation to deliver reports of the KVM to the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; although, this was an express provision of the agreement. I also had the honour to tell Your Honours that we presented this problem to the chairperson of the Ministry of the -- of Foreign Affairs of Sweden, Mr. Vollebaek, in early January, 1999. And even after that intervention, which is documented and which is presented to Your Honours, there was no compliance with this provision by the OSCE.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was the visit to Vollebaek made in connection with his impending assumption of office at the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Minister Vollebaek, the chairperson of the OSCE, visited Belgrade just a few days after taking over the chairmanship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yesterday, though, we read of arrangements being made for a visit with a Minister of Foreign Affairs of Sweden, I think. Now, was that a visit that Mr. Sainovic actually paid to Sweden, or was it the reception of a delegation from Sweden in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I don't remember Mr. Sainovic travelling to Sweden. I do know that he visited Belgium and the European Union and Austria.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, Witness Sandra Mitchell, who testified in this case, told us of the KVM system of reporting on a weekly basis to the head office, and these reports became available to the Member States. Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of what I stated before Your Honours, and that is that reports of the KVM were not delivered to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and that the OSCE thus violated an express provision of the agreement. If there are any indicia, or if there is any evidence to the contrary, I would be very happy to look at it and comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, just to go back to the point I asked you about a moment ago, do you still have the binder of documents there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.
