utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you look at that tab 28, which is 2D183. Is that not about a visit that Mr. Sainovic was to pay to Sweden and Denmark?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this relates to a planned visit of Mr. Sainovic to Denmark and Sweden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did it not take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I remember correctly, that visit did not actually take place. I can't recall the precise reason why it did not materialise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown -- sorry. You were shown the agreement that you signed with Mr. Geremek on the 19th of October, 1998, in which --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Perhaps my friend would help me with the tab number. The witness is looking for it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's P432, but I --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's tab number 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you referred to item 3, section 1, which reads that: "The verification mission will travel throughout Kosovo to verify the maintenance of the cease-fire by all elements. It will investigate reports of cease-fire violations. Mission personnel will have full freedom of movement and access throughout Kosovo at all times." Now, you were saying that you did not -- you said that you did not know what cease-fire was being referred to; and as far as you're concerned, access or movement throughout Kosovo at all times did not include access to VJ or MUP barracks or weapons disposition, armouries. You also said that this agreement should be read in context with other agreements that existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The way the question was put by Mr. Stamp implies that there are two questions, in fact, contained in that question, and the first one is incorrect. Mr. Stamp is saying that Witness Jovanovic said that he did not know the word "cease-fire" was mentioned in the agreement he drafted. He didn't say that. Let's not have two questions in one. He knows his agreement off by heart, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was not implying that he did not know the word "cease-fire" was in the agreement, but witness did say --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- did you not, Mr. Jovanovic, that you didn't know what cease-fire they were talking about in the agreement, what cease-fire was being referred to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. He did say that, Mr. Stamp, that's correct. So please proceed with the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- know that - sorry - the UN Security Council Resolution 1199 called on all parties to cease hostilities, and in particular Yugoslavia to cease all actions by security forces affecting the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In addition to that, do you not know of an agreement signed by Mr. Sainovic in which he -- or the agreement provided that combined police, special police trained in Kosovo, would be reduced to their February 1998 duty level? This is P395 I'm referring to. Did you know of that agreement, that there's an agreement? It's not in your folder, I don't think. I'm just asking if you know of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am an I a signatory of the agreement or a participant?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, you're not.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with that document, but I do know that it was agreed that the military and police presence in Kosovo and Metohija was to be reduced, and this is also mentioned in the Moscow declaration which was accepted or agreed on much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And this was also a matter that the KVM observer team were responsible to verify?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, as a Minister of Foreign Affairs, all the KVM powers and competencies are contained solely in the agreement I signed with the chairman, Geremek, not on the 19th of October --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- but on the 16th of October. No other provisions existed for me in the capacity of federal minister, nor was it my responsibility to deal with anything beyond the agreement I signed with Chairman Geremek. All my obligations are contained in that document -- or rather, the obligations of the government I represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the provisions --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- I understand that. Didn't you say that this document that you signed should be read along with other agreements in place at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document I signed with Mr. Geremek was self-explanatory. It does not refer to any other agreements or accords.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Just listen to me, Mr. Jovanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a page reference for this statement that you're making that he said it had to be read in conjunction with other agreements?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not right now, Your Honour, but I could find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it is the quick way of getting to the point in these situations, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Anyway, do you recall saying that, and -- do you recall saying that? And this needs a yes or no answer. Was it your position yesterday that this agreement had to be read in context with existing agreements at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This agreement should be read in the light of the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement of the 12th of October, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it the position of the FRY, in 1998 and 1999, that this Tribunal would have jurisdiction over war crimes that might have been committed in the FRY after 1993? Was that the position on the FRY?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The position on the FRY was formulated at the time of the Dayton-Paris Agreement, which said that the sides would cooperate in discovering and prosecuting crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And would cooperate with this Tribunal? That's what the question is about. Wasn't it the position of the FRY, when you were Foreign Minister, that the FRY would cooperate with this Tribunal? Again that question can be answered, "Yes, it was," or, "No, it was not."

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall, however, saying, in 2001 or 2002, after you relinquished office, that the hand-over of President Milosevic to this Tribunal would be, to quote you, "the ultimate treason"? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I see the reference for that? Can this be shown?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's find out if the witness recognise this first of all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you recall saying, in 2001 or 2002, that the hand-over of President Milosevic to this Tribunal would be, in your words, "the ultimate treason"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I spoke at many public gatherings, and I cannot remember all the expressions I used; but, in general, I advocated the position that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in cooperation with The Hague Tribunal, is bound to respect its own constitution and its own laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you recall saying that to hand over President Milosevic to the Tribunal would be -- would amount to the ultimate treason? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't have anything further for this witness. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll try and do it in three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you're under no pressure. It's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, no. [Interpretation] We'll see how it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, one of Mr. Stamp's question was when Yugoslavia's membership in the OSCE was suspended, but you were interrupted when you were replying. Can you tell me when this happened?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in 1992 at the OSC conference in Budapest when the suspension of the membership rights of the FRY was done by violating the principle of consensus, and almost inexplicably the position was adopted of consensus minus one.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And how long did this situation last?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the political changes that took place in Serbia in the year 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a clarify that. Was it the FRY's membership that was suspended, or was it the Socialist Federal Republic's membership that was suspended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The membership rights of Yugoslavia were suspended because, at that time, the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was breaking up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor asked you about crimes against -- or rather, crimes committed by Serbs in 1998. Do you know of a single crime committed by Serbs in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps Obrinje?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the name from the media, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Nothing else?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Do you remember crimes against Serbs; for example, Klecka, Radonjic -- or Lake Radonjic?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember these crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. And my last question, and then we'll have a break: The Prosecutor asked you whether Sainovic reported to you about his contacts and conversations while he was at Kosovo. Was it his duty to inform you of who he was meeting and what he was talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. He used professionals from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as logistics, and they sent reports after every conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And if he spoke to, for example, a municipal president, did he have to inform you of that?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not have to, and he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And this refers to the army, the police?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, the re-examination moved so speedily in Serbian that I could not interpose an objection in respect to the question at line 58, 1, that prefaced by saying that I asked Mr. Sainovic whether he reported to Mr. Jovanovic. I did not ask Mr. Sainovic whether he reported to Mr. Jovanovic. But the thing is that the answer is "yes," which raises something quite new which did not flow from anything I asked. And if the answer is yes, he reported to Mr. Jovanovic, I would ask to inquire further into that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila, what do you have to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are two types of contacts in question. When Sainovic had contacts with diplomats, he used the services of the outposts and he spoke about this to Mr. Jovanovic, but my question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't want you to explain things of that nature in the presence of the witness. The question is: Do you have any objection to Mr. Stamp exploring further the communications that took place from Sainovic to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we will do that after we've had the break. Again, please, Mr. Jovanovic, would you leave the courtroom with the usher, and you should return -- well, you'll come back at 10 minutes to 1.00, when we shall resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, or who is taking over?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp is on his way down. I'm trying to reach him at present, if we could just have a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He normally returns, Mr. Jovanovic. I doubt if you've scored a direct hit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not that malicious, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, he's just on his way down. I apologise for the slight delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I do apologise. Somehow I got the times mixed up. I think we've been having the long day so often I assumed it was a one-hour break, and that is how --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope you're not suffering from indigestion. We shall allow you to explore the matter you raised at the end of the last session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I understand or it seemed to me what you were saying, and tell me if I am right, is that you were saying Mr. Sainovic had a duty or obligation to make -- to report to you?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid, with all due respect, that you misunderstood me. I respect that you're busy with a number of different subjects, but you misunderstood me. The deputy prime minister does not, as a rule, submit reports to any minister in the government. However, what is at stake here is information and conversations that Deputy Prime Minister Sainovic had with foreign diplomats in Kosovo and Metohija or elsewhere, for that matter. These reports were produced by professionals employed by the Federal Foreign Ministry, and these were the people providing the logistics it, as it were, in addition to the deputy prime minister. [In English] These are not reports but information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And it's information about the activities and foreign affairs on the diplomatic front; is that correct? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think I misunderstood your answer before the break. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, it's a political science [Realtime transcript read in error "politicised"] question more than anything else. I was wondering how did you arrive at a consensus within the cabinet and how deliberations went there on issues for the relevant time which was very crucial and tumultuous and all things were brought in and how were these resolved? If you could throw some light on the working of the cabinet, that's very kind and thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, I would like to say that Kosovo and Metohija is the single most important state and national problem in both Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. A consensus always existed about this issue, even prior to the democratic changes in 2000; just as today, there is a consensus by all major political parties in Serbia on ways to find a peaceful political solution. There were no substantial differences as far as essential issues were concerned between the different members of the government, members of the cabinet, or between the different ministries. They -- there may have been subtle differences but never any disagreement on the essence of the entire problem. Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia always wanted to achieve a lasting peace and stability in that part of South-east Europe, in that part of Serbia and Yugoslavia. The cabinet was fully aware that this was the only way forward to greater economic prosperity and stability, and that only in this way would Serbia soon be on its way to Europe and to the renewal of its membership in all European and international organisations. There was the awareness that peace in Kosovo and Metohija was a precondition of any future prosperity in Yugoslavia, and this awareness existed throughout my time as a member of the cabinet. As a citizen of Serbia, I do have to express my deep satisfaction that such a consensus exists even as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: When there was an agreement at Rambouillet, was it brought to the attention of the cabinet; and if so, did the cabinet take a decision on that and was that voiced? Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may strike you as my personal private position, but it was the position of my government, the cabinet of which I was a member. There was no agreement that was reached in Rambouillet. It is a pleasure to hear that Your Honour is inquiring about the political and social aspects, which gives me an opportunity to say this: Any agreement implies a consensus and goodwill on the part of all parties to negotiations. In Paris and in Rambouillet, there was no consensus, regrettably I have to say, since Rambouillet was later used as a pretext for NATO's aggression against Yugoslavia. As for Rambouillet, I personally submitted a report to the federal government about the problems and about the substance of the talks. There is an official document which is included in this set of documents, and this reflects accurately what position were is taken by the federal government vis-a-vis the report. Nothing about the so-called negotiations at Rambouillet and Paris, nothing about the positions taken by Serbia and Yugoslavia, was a secret, a secret for the public in Serbia or for the international public for that matter. All information was accessible: The strategies, the various causes, and the various problems. I believe this is the situation that still prevails today. I sincerely hope that this clarity will contribute to a lasting peaceful solution, which would be a good reflection of the efforts made by Serbia as we speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Jovanovic, you may have misunderstood a part of that question. There were elements of the Rambouillet agreement on which there were no differences. Were these, on which there was some agreement, considered by the cabinet, and I think Judge Chowhan was anxious to know what the cabinet's reaction was. Did they approve of these or was there a different view taken among any members of the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: ZIVADIN JOVANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the federal government was the recipient of a full, extensive analysis and a very thorough information on both what happened in Rambouillet and Paris and on the result and the substance of the document conditionally referred to as the Rambouillet agreement. By your leave, and this may be an unacceptable thing for me to say, but the agreement exists as a whole or not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. There is one other minor matter to resolve. Line 61 -- sorry, page 61, line 2, the question Judge Chowhan asked was prefaced by the words it's a "political science question," not "a politicised question."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Mr. Jovanovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming here to give us the benefit of your involvement in these various events. You are now free to leave. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our next witness is Milan Jovanovic. He's somewhere in the Tribunal building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There was some question over the 65 ter notice in relation to him. Is there any -- Mr. Stamp, there was a request to amend the 65 ter notice in relation to the next witness in relation to that? Is there any problem with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll allow that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic. You should have earphones, I think, if -- good afternoon, Mr. Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading allowed the document which you will now be shown.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. You will now be examined by Mr. Fila on behalf of Mr. Sainovic. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Can you state your name, please. Share your personal information with us, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Milan Jovanovic. I was born on the 12th of March 1958 in Tuzla. I went to elementary and secondary school in Lukavac in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I graduated, took my MA degree and my Ph.D. at the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade. Having completed my education, I worked at the Institute for Political Research, and I worked for a number of different political organisations. For four years, I worked as the director of the -- the republican directorate for property of the Republic of Serbia. I was also the manager of the public company of the Official Gazette of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Since 1998, I have been working at the Faculty of Political Sciences, which is attached to the Belgrade University. I am an associate professor, and I teach a subject called "Serbia's Political System."

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What did you do in the Socialist Party of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since its very foundation, I have performed different tasks in the party. Between 1990 and 1993, I worked as a consultant in the Commission for Theoretical Work and an advisor to the Committee for Foreign Affairs. I was also the chef de cabinet of the deputy president of the SPS. Between 1993 and 2000, I worked as secretary of the Technical Services Section for the Main Board of the SPS. This is a position that I, as expert, was appointed to the Executive Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about your involvement in the SPS? Was it a professional involvement or a political one?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was professional. For a brief while in 2000, between the 4th and the 5th Congresses, I was also a member of the Main and Executive Boards of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did you attend meetings of the Main Board, the Executive Board, or any other very important Working Groups or bodies of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I attended meetings of the Main and Executive Boards between 1993 and 2000. I attended most of the sessions. In my capacity as secretary, before the Technical Services, I was duty-bound to attend. I had close ties to the Secretary-General of the SPS who headed the Executive Board. It was for this reason that I was involved in the work of these bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So what about the Main Board do as opposed to the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As opposed to the Main Board, the Executive Board was the executive body of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were minutes taken at the meetings of the Main Board and the Executive Board of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Minutes were taken and records were drawn up from the meetings of the Main Board and the Executive Board of the SPS. These are documents that at every meeting of the Main Board or the Executive Board would first be adopted. The minutes from the previous meeting would first be adopted because they reflected any discussion that took place during that previous meeting; therefore, these documents were then adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: In relation to the position which you held in the SPS, did you have any insight into the documents, the developments, and the political ideas of the SPS at the time you spent working there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had an insight into all the essential political documents of the SPS at the time. I was directly involved in producing many drafts and documents of many different kinds, starting with various types of analysis, presentations, communiques, the statute itself; therefore, I am familiar with all of the SPS's policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: How were these communiques or announcements following meetings of the Main Board and Executive Board of the SPS produced?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Most frequently, I was directly involved in the drafting and production of these documents. Our bodies in the SPS, the Main Board and the Executive Board, our bodies were a great number of members. The Main Board comprised up to 250 people, and the Executive Board comprised up to 35 persons. The various Working Groups or bodies would normally number between 20 and 50 members. The official communiques or announcements would always reflect the gist of what was discussed at any of the meetings. It was simply impossible for one thing to be discussed and another to be communicated; and after all, there was no need for that. The SPS was a party organised along democratic lines and not some sort of conspiratorial cell. If you bear in mind the fact that very often a large number of vice-presidents, presidents and secretaries were involved in these bodies - I'm talking about municipal level, the district level, and the provincial level, the boards at municipal provincial and district levels - then it becomes clear that a large number of people were involved in the drafting of those documents. The concept of a mass party, the party for the masses, implies that we have permanent communication with our boards. The boards were sending all sorts of contributions to the headquarters of the party, and they always reacted positively to our communiques. They related to all our positions. They could relate to all our positions. Had that not been the case, they certainly would have raised some -- some sort of a protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And now for the benefit of the Chamber and everybody else listening, can you please briefly explain the way the SPS was organised, specifically the Main Board and the Executive Board. How exactly did that work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Congress is the supreme body of the SPS. The Congress would meet once every four years or earlier if needed. At the Congress, a president would be elected, the Main Board, and the statutory and supervisory commission. Between any two Congress meetings, the Main Board was the supreme body of the party. It appointed the members of the Executive Board, the Secretary-General, and all the vice-presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Were there any commissions or such like?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Board would appoint members to all these various bodies, such as commissions, councils, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who had the power to make nominations for the post of vice-president of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The person with the power to do that under the statute was the president of the Socialist Party of Serbia. He was the principal proposer, in a manner of speaking, and he had sole right to nominate candidates and table these nominations to the Main Board. He could also propose what powers they might or might not have, and he could also propose that certain people be dismissed from that post.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We know that this person was Slobodan Milosevic, so what was his influence on the overall activity and work of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: President Slobodan Milosevic enjoyed a large degree of authority and influence over the work of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he chair any of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So how were conclusions adopted by the Main Board of the SPS?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Before every meeting, certain persons were appointed to make reports in different fields; usually, it was the Secretary-General or some of the members of the Main Board or Executive Board who was well-versed in terms of the subjects that were discussed, that were on the agenda. These rapporteurs had the role of moderators as well during the debate. They familiarised the board with the items that were on the agenda; and then after their reports, there would be a debate, sometimes longer, sometimes shorter. Once the debate was over, it would be summarised by the president of the party, Slobodan Milosevic. Conclusions were proposed by the rapporteurs and by the participants in the discussion; however, he finally summarised the discussion and proposed conclusions to the Main Board. The Main Board would state its views by way of a vote, and then the conclusions would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the dominant subject in this period of time that we're talking about, in this period of 1998, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that period, the dominant subject was the situation in Kosovo and Metohija: The economic situation, the activities of the government, and of our parliamentary group in the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about the Executive Board of the SPS? What did they do and what did they take decisions on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Executive Board had up to 35 members. All of them individually had specific assignments in specific fields, and they followed the work of district and municipal committees. It mainly dealt with carrying out decisions by the Main Board. The Executive Board made its decisions through public ballot, and they were as a rule adopted unanimously. Slobodan Milosevic did not chair meetings of the Executive Board. That was done bit Secretary-General of the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What about regional representation in the Executive Board? Were there representatives from all parts of the country?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you to explain to us the participation of the SPS in government and in coalitions at the level of the republic and at the level of the federation in the period up to 1999 -- the end of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: After the first elections in 1990, when the SPS formed a single party government, all other elections resulted in a way that led to the creation of coalition governments. After the elections in 1992, there was a minority government whose term was short; and then after 1993, a government was formed with the party called New Democracy, one of the coalition partners parties Depos coalition. After the 1997 elections, at the level of the Republic of Serbia, a broader coalition was formed. There was a national unity government with the Serb Radical Party and the Yugoslav Left, respectively. At federal level, from the very moment the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was constituted, there were coalition governments. As for the other republic that was a member of the federation, that is to say Montenegro, the coalition partner was the Democratic Party of Socialists. After the split in that party in 1997, the SPS formed a coalition with the Socialist Party, The Socialist People's Party from Montenegro, a political party that advocated the further existence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Different coalitions at federal and republican levels required a subtle pursuit of policy and far more tolerance within the legislation and government because a broader consensus had to be built in order for decisions to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: As you already said, Kosovo and Metohija were always a priority in SPS activities. How did it come about that a Main Board session was held on the 10th [Realtime transcript read in error "12th"] of June, 1998?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The word used was "Kosovo and Metohija were always a priority in SPS activities," and that's in line 21. Yes. Please answer the question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That session was held in an atmosphere when there was an escalation of terrorist attacks in Kosovo and Metohija. Every day there were news about attacks against public institutions, about assassinations of public servants, police, the military, post offices, waterworks, et cetera. The terrorists blocked roads; and, in this way, practically blocked 40 per cent of the territory of that province. Every day they placed roadblocks on these roads, kidnapped citizens, murdered them, and wounded them. Such news were coming in every day from that region. Many citizens were forced to leave their homes, which was the objective of the terrorists. Every day, from the Albanian border, large quantities of war materiel and weapons were brought in from the Republic of Albanians, which showed that the terrorists were preparing an escalation of conflict in the province. The right assessment would be that panic prevailed among the citizens, and they raised the question of whether the state was capable of protecting them and insuring a normal peaceful life in the province and whether indeed the date wanted to do that. In this kind of an atmosphere, the session that you mentioned was held, the session of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: What was the position of Serbs in the territory of Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The position of Serbs in the territory of Metohija was such that they were the most threatened ethnic group. However, terrorists were displaying violence against the members of other ethnic groups as well, including Albanians who did not want to join them and who remained loyal to the policy of and the state of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: I have a problem with the transcript. The transcript says that the special was held on the "12th," and it was actually held on the 10th of June, 1998. Do you have that binder?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was here, but I don't see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he please have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Could you please look at tab 12 now. P1012 is the exhibit number, and could you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a joint proposal --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sorry. There's been some kind of a mistake. That's not it. I am sorry. Wrong number. I am sorry. There has been a mistake in terms of the numbers. Yes. Now we're going to have a look at -- it is tab 8. Sorry. Mistake. Tab 8.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These are minutes of the 16th Session of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia held on the 10th of June 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The first question I'd like to put to you is: Who made the introductory report, and how did the debate develop at that session?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Three reports were submitted there by Gorica Gajevic, Secretary-General; Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic; and as for the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, a report was made by Milomir Minic.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Who was what?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the Main Board of the Socialist Party of Serbia and of the Executive Board in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did he have a particular position in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was president of the Chamber of citizens in the national assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sainovic present, and did he take part in debate at this session where Kosovo was discussed?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was present, but he did not take part in the debate.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now what the conclusions were that were reached by that particular meeting of the Main Board of the SPS? Could you look at page 3 of the minutes, and could you tell us then what the ways and means were for finding a solution to this?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This session of the Main Board was practically -- practically adopted a platform for the policy of the SPS vis-a-vis Kosovo and Metohija. Briefly, it was based on a few fundamental principles: First, that all problems have to be resolved by peaceful means, political means, through direct dialogue among all the ethnic communities living in Kosovo and Metohija. Furthermore, that dialogues should start straight away without any pre-conditions. Thirdly, that a solution for Kosovo and Metohija should be based on a broadest possible autonomy that would take into account all standards pertaining to human rights, civic rights, and the rights of national minorities, too. In this way, it would fully be in line with documents adopted by international organisations. Also, this was supposed to be organised in a way that would prevent the possibility of any kind of out-voting or discrimination on ethnic grounds. The next principle pertained to condemning violence as a method of attaining political goals. And, finally, that platform contained a position stating that the international community was called upon in order to include Serbia and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in international integration processes as soon as possible, because this would send a signal to the terrorists that violence would not be tolerated in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: European processes?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: European and international.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The Main Board of the SPS, at this meeting of the 10th of June, 1998, did it make any special decisions? Could you look at page 4, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Main Board established a Working Group in order to speed up a solution for Kosovo and Metohija. It consists of Milomir Minic, Dusko Matkovic, and Zoran Andjelkovic. I already mentioned that the first person was a member of the Main Board, the Executive Board, president of the Chamber of citizens of the Federal Assembly. Mr. Matkovic was vice-president of the Socialist Party of Serbia, a Member of Parliament, and the director of a big company, the Smederevo Steelworks. Zoran Andjelkovic was a member of the Main Board, an MP, and a minister and activist with a lot of experience on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And who headed this group?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Milomir Minic headed this group.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: That can be seen from the text.

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, earlier in your evidence, you said that Working Groups normally consisted of 20 to 50 members. Was this a very unusual Working Group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was referring to the councils and commissions of the Main Board. These were broader bodies charged with various areas, such as agriculture, foreign affairs, health care, welfare, and so on, and they were more numerous. These were permanent working bodies, either of the Main Board or of the Executive Board. The Main Board set up Working Groups like this one whenever there were problems in a certain domain. That's why this was not unusual, and this was the number of members such groups usually had.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Does it say here that it can be broadened? Would you read what it says?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a possibility here for this group to be extended and to include cadres from other parts of the republic. This was done in a particular way. Each district committee was in charge of a certain area in cooperation with our party committees in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Why was this set up?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The main reason why this Working Group was set up was to seek a political solution in Kosovo and Metohija, to calm down the situation, and to find a way of solving the issues. This team which joined them was working on the strength of their political and personal authority in Kosovo and Metohija. They carried out consultations, talked to citizens, various party fora. They were not in a position to suspend or substitute other existing state or party organs in Kosovo. They were simply there to assist them in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And what was their obligation towards the party headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Their duty was to submit regular reports on their work to the party headquarters, as well as report on the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, the standpoints expressed by the citizens and activists they met, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Would you please tell us how long this team spent in Kosovo and Metohija? How long was it there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This team spent the most time in Kosovo and Metohija in the course of the summer, until the end of the anti-terrorist activities in September. After that time, there was no longer an intense need for their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You mentioned anti-terrorist actions. When was this and what were the consequences?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: These anti-terrorist actions took place in September, and they led to the pacifying of the situation in Kosovo and Metohija so that there was no longer any need for the activity of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: After the end of these anti-terrorist operations, were some sort of agreements reached in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Agreements were concluded between Milosevic and Holbrooke, Jovanovic and Geremek. The arrival of the verification of the OSCE was imminent, and the situation became calmer. One could see a political outcome ahead, a political denouement. So there was no longer any need for that team to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, when was the last time the team spent in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: In late October. I think that was the last time they visited Kosovo and Metohija. They attended a session of the Regional Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: A SPS Regional Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was that the end of their work?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the end of their work; although, in the course of September, the team had been a lot less active because they had other obligations also. So they visited Kosovo and Metohija less often.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Was this team in any functional connection with other state organs or individuals engaged in official business for the state or was it only linked to the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. This team was exclusively connected to the organs of the Socialist Party of Serbia in functional terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Did any of these three members of the team that you mentioned remain in Kosovo and Metohija after what you said, after October 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Zoran Andjelkovic remained but in the capacity of president of the Executive Board. He was appointed by the national assembly of the Republic of Serbia to that position. From that point on, he was a state official and no longer had any party tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: So when he was appointed by the national assembly he became the president of the regional Executive Board. That was a provisional Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILAN JOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a few more questions, but I think this might be a convenient moment to break for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you say a "few more," you're not near the end of the examination, are you, or are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I'm not far from the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Jovanovic, we have to end our session for the day at this time because this court is occupied now by another case. That means, regrettably, that you have to come back tomorrow. That will be at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's very important that overnight, between now and coming back here, you have no discussions with anyone about the evidence in this case. You can discuss anything else with whoever you like, but you must have no discussion about anyone at all about the evidence. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will see you again tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, there was just one other matter. It may be only Mr. Hannis knows the answer, but there's been a recent application by Mr. Fila for videolink in relation to another of his witnesses who has suffered recent incapacity. Do you know yet whether the Prosecution have anything to say on that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We are just making one inquiry. We probably will have an answer this afternoon later tomorrow and indicate our position then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well if you could convey the answer when you get it we should be in a position to get it with a view to that evidence being taken at the same time as the other videolink evidence if appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 9.00 tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of August, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.
